video_caption: The video opens with a celestial scene, showcasing a ringed planet (Saturn) on the right against a dark, star-filled space with a bright, flaring star in the upper left from 0:00 to 0:08. This transitions into a view of Earth rotating slowly amidst faint nebulae and a similar bright star with a lens flare, from 0:08 to 0:14. From 0:14 to 0:22, an orange-red screen appears with contact information: "CONTACT PROF. JIM CAFFEY" (top left) and "Contact:" (top right), listing "ProfessorJimCaffey@gmail.com" (with Gmail icon), "in Jim Caffey" (with LinkedIn icon), "f Science Professor Jim Caffey Page," "f The Astronomers Group," "f The Space Place Group" (all with Facebook icons), "▶ ProfessorJimCaffey" (with YouTube icon), and "@ProfessorCaffey" (with Twitter icon). A photo of Professor Jim Caffey, a man with short brown hair, smiling and wearing a blue polo shirt, is displayed on the left against a dark red background. This then changes to a dark red title screen from 0:22 to 0:28, which reads: "WELCOME TO 10-MINUTE ASTRONOMY! WITH PROFESSOR JIM CAFFEY" (top left), "Episode 3 Chapter 1 A Tour of the Universe, The Nature of Science and Astronomy, Numbers in Astronomy" (top right). Below, two images are presented: the left shows "Comet Hyakutake - March 20, 1996 Taken with 24-Inch Wide-Field Burrell Schmidt Telescope Kitt Peak National Observatory, Tucson, Arizona USA Image by Astronomy Instructor Jim Caffey," depicting a vibrant, colorful comet with a long tail; the right image shows another comet in a star-filled sky next to an observatory dome. Finally, from 0:28 to 0:40, the screen splits: the left side is grey with an "openstax" logo, and the right side shows Professor Jim Caffey, a man with short brown hair and a headset with a microphone, sitting in a room with a cluttered background including a couch, rug, and sleeping dog. He is wearing a blue collared shirt and directly addresses the camera, introducing himself as "Professor Jim Caffey" and stating that this is the "lecture video for Astronomy," with an audio distortion occurring during the last word. A "logi" (Logitech) logo is visible in the bottom right corner of his video frame.

The video features a bearded man in a dark shirt, visible in a small frame at the bottom right, presenting a slideshow. The initial slide is titled "ASTRONOMY" (English: ASTRONOMY) in green, with the subtitle "Chapter 1 SCIENCE AND THE UNIVERSE: A BRIEF TOUR" (English: Chapter 1 SCIENCE AND THE UNIVERSE: A BRIEF TOUR) and "PowerPoint Image Slideshow" (English: PowerPoint Image Slideshow). A blue book cover titled "Introduction to Astronomy" (English: Introduction to Astronomy) is prominently displayed in the center. The slide then transitions to "FIGURE 1.1" (English: FIGURE 1.1), showcasing a captivating image of two spiral galaxies, rendered in vibrant blues, whites, and yellows, seemingly interacting against a dark cosmic backdrop. Below the image, a green heading "Distant Galaxies" (English: Distant Galaxies) is followed by descriptive text that reads, "These two interacting islands of stars (galaxies) are so far away that their light takes hundreds of millions of years to reach us on Earth (photographed with the Hubble Space Telescope), (credit: modification of work by NASA, ESA, the Hubble Heritage (STScI/AURA)-ESA/Hubble Collaboration, and K. Noll (STScI))." (English: These two interacting islands of stars (galaxies) are so far away that their light takes hundreds of millions of years to reach us on Earth (photographed with the Hubble Space Telescope), (credit: modification of work by NASA, ESA, the Hubble Heritage (STScI/AURA)-ESA/Hubble Collaboration, and K. Noll (STScI)).) The presenter actively speaks and gestures with his hands while looking at the content on the screen.

In the video segment from 0:04 to 0:05, a man with a beard and glasses, wearing a dark blue t-shirt, is visible in the bottom right corner, looking and gesturing towards the main presentation slide. The slide, titled "FIGURE 1.2," displays a large image of Mars against a black background. A yellow circular annotation briefly highlights a prominent canyon system on Mars. Below the image, the text "Mars Mosaic. This image of Mars is centered on the Valles Marineris (Mariner Valley) complex of canyons, which is as long as the United States is wide. (credit: modification of work by NASA)" is displayed. The OpenStax logo is present in the top right corner of the slide.

A man with a beard and dark hair is visible in a small window at the bottom right, speaking while looking towards a presentation slide on the main screen. The slide features a vibrant image of the Orion Nebula, a colorful cloud of cosmic gas and dust, on the right. To the left of the image, text describes the Orion Nebula as "a beautiful cloud of cosmic raw material (gas and dust from which new stars and planets are being made)," located "about 1400 light-years away," and highlights that "the gas and dust in this region are illuminated by the intense light from a few extremely energetic adolescent stars." A yellow circle briefly highlights a central bright area in the nebula image around the 0:07 mark. The top of the slide displays the "openstax" logo on the left and "FIGURE 1.4" on the right.

The video segment shows a presentation slide with a man presenting via webcam in the bottom right corner. From 0:05 to 0:31, the slide displays "FIGURE 1.6" in green at the top left and the "openstax" logo at the top right. The main image is a vibrant view of Earth's Western Hemisphere from space, featuring blue oceans, green landmasses, and white clouds against a black background. Below the image, green text reads: "Humanity's Home Base. This image shows the Western hemisphere as viewed from space 35,400 kilometers (about 22,000 miles) above Earth. Data about the land surface from one satellite was combined with another satellite's data about the clouds to create the image. (credit: modification of work by R. Stockli, A. Nelson, F. Hasler, NASA/GSFC/NOAA/USGS)". The presenter, a man with dark hair and a beard wearing a dark t-shirt, gestures with his hands as he speaks, and a yellow circle briefly highlights parts of the text at the bottom. At 0:31, the slide transitions to "FIGURE 1.7" with the same "openstax" logo. The central image is now a long black rectangle containing a small blue and white sphere representing Earth on the far left, and an even smaller white/gray sphere representing the Moon on the far right, illustrating their relative sizes and distance to scale. The accompanying green text at the bottom states: "Earth and Moon, Drawn to Scale. This image shows Earth and the Moon shown to scale for both size and distance. (credit: modification of work by NASA)". The man continues to present, looking at the screen and occasionally gesturing.

The video segment opens with a man, sporting a beard and dark hair and wearing a dark long-sleeved shirt, visible in the bottom right corner, looking at the screen and gesturing with his right hand as he speaks. The main part of the screen displays a slide titled "FIGURE 1.8" (English: FIGURE 1.8), featuring an illustration of "Our Solar Family." The image depicts a large, bright yellow sun on the left, followed by the planets Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune, all labeled and drawn to scale, grouped under "Planets" (English: Planets). Further right and slightly below, smaller celestial bodies named Ceres, Pluto, Haumea, Makemake, and Eris are shown, grouped under "Dwarf planets" (English: Dwarf planets), against a black background. Below the image, text reads: "Our Solar Family. The Sun, the planets, and some dwarf planets are shown with their sizes drawn to scale. The orbits of the planets are much more widely separated than shown in this drawing. Notice the size of Earth compared to the giant planets. (credit: modification of work by NASA)" (English: Our Solar Family. The Sun, the planets, and some dwarf planets are shown with their sizes drawn to scale. The orbits of the planets are much more widely separated than shown in this drawing. Notice the size of Earth compared to the giant planets. (credit: modification of work by NASA)). An "openstax" (English: openstax) logo is in the top right, and the slide background has colorful vertical and horizontal stripes. At 0:29, the slide transitions to "FIGURE 1.9" (English: FIGURE 1.9), which shows a vibrant spiral galaxy, NGC 1073, against a dark starry background. The accompanying text reads: "Spiral Galaxy. This galaxy of billions of stars, called by its catalog number NGC 1073, is thought to be similar to our own Milky Way Galaxy. Here we see the giant wheel-shaped system with a bar of stars across its middle. (credit: NASA, ESA)" (English: Spiral Galaxy. This galaxy of billions of stars, called by its catalog number NGC 1073, is thought to be similar to our own Milky Way Galaxy. Here we see the giant wheel-shaped system with a bar of stars across its middle. (credit: NASA, ESA)). The man continues to speak and gesture briefly as the video segment ends.

A man in a dark t-shirt is visible in the bottom right corner, gesturing with his hands as he presents two distinct images of galaxies. From 00:03 to 00:20, the screen displays "FIGURE 1.9" and the "openstax" logo, along with an image of a spiral galaxy (NGC 1073) featuring a prominent central bar and spiral arms. A yellow circle highlights various parts of the galaxy as the presenter explains the bright areas are gas and new stars, while the dark streaks are dust. The accompanying text reads: "Spiral Galaxy. This galaxy of billions of stars, called by its catalog number NGC 1073, is thought to be similar to our own Milky Way Galaxy. Here we see the giant wheel-shaped system with a bar of stars across its middle. (credit: NASA, ESA)". At 00:20, the slide transitions to "FIGURE 1.10," showing a breathtaking night landscape with the silhouette of a person standing on a hill, gazing up at the Milky Way galaxy stretching across the sky, with an orange glow near the horizon. The text for this image states: "Milky Way Galaxy. Because we are inside the Milky Way Galaxy, we see its disk in cross-section flung across the sky like a great milky white avenue of stars with dark "rifts" of dust. In this dramatic image, part of it is seen above Trona Pinnacles in the California desert. (credit: Ian Norman)".

A bearded man with dark hair, wearing a dark top, is positioned in the bottom right corner of the frame, actively speaking. The main view is a presentation slide featuring a colorful vertical stripe pattern on the left edge. The top left corner displays "FIGURE 1.10" in green text, while the OpenStax logo is in the top right. A prominent image dominates the left side of the slide, depicting a breathtaking night sky with the Milky Way galaxy stretching across it as a luminous, cloudy band, above the silhouette of a person standing on a desert landscape with a glowing horizon. To the right of this image, a text caption describes it as the "Milky Way Galaxy," explaining that its disk is seen in cross-section with "dark 'rifts' of dust," captured above the Trona Pinnacles in the California desert, credited to Ian Norman. The background behind the speaking man is blurred, showing what appears to be an indoor setting with bookshelves.

The video opens with a slide titled "FIGURE 1.11" featuring the "openstax™" logo. The left side of the slide displays text in a white box: "Star Cluster. This large star cluster is known by its catalog number, M9. It contains some 250,000 stars and is seen more clearly from space using the Hubble Space Telescope. It is located roughly 25,000 light-years away. (credit: NASA, ESA)". To the right, a detailed image shows a dense, spherical star cluster, appearing as a multitude of bright white and yellow dots against a dark, star-filled background. In the bottom right corner of the screen, a man with a beard and short dark hair is visible, actively speaking and gesturing with his hands as if giving a presentation. Around the 0:19 mark, the slide transitions to "FIGURE 1.12," which features the text "Neighbor Galaxies. This image shows both the Large Magellanic Cloud and the Small Magellanic Cloud above the telescopes of the Atacama Large Millimeter/Submillimeter Array (ALMA) in the Atacama Desert of northern Chile. (credit: ESO, C. Malin)". The accompanying image depicts a nighttime scene with a row of large, dish-shaped radio telescopes in the foreground under a star-studded sky, with two luminous, cloud-like galaxies visible above them. The man continues to speak and gesture in the bottom right.

A man with a beard and dark short-sleeved shirt is visible in a small video feed in the bottom right corner of the screen, gesturing with his hands while speaking. The main portion of the screen displays a slideshow presentation with a colorful striped border on the left, top, and right sides, and an "openstax" logo in the top right corner. The first slide shown features the text "FIGURE 1.12" at the top and an image of several large satellite dishes (telescopes) under a dark, starry night sky, with two cloud-like galaxies visible above them. The caption below reads: "Neighbor Galaxies. This image shows both the Large Magellanic Cloud and the Small Magellanic Cloud above the telescopes of the Atacama Large Millimeter/Submillimeter Array (ALMA) in the Atacama Desert of northern Chile. (credit: ESO, C. Malin)". At 0:21, the slide changes to "FIGURE 1.13," displaying a large, glowing spiral galaxy (the Andromeda galaxy) against a black background filled with tiny stars. The accompanying text states: "Closest Spiral Galaxy. The Andromeda galaxy (M31) is a spiral-shaped collection of stars similar to our own Milky Way. (credit: Adam Evans)". At 0:54, the slide transitions to "FIGURE 1.14," which shows a dense field of numerous galaxies of various shapes and sizes, appearing as bright pinpoints and small smudges of light against a black cosmic backdrop. The caption explains: "Fornax Cluster of Galaxies. In this image, you can see part of a cluster of galaxies located about 60 million light-years away in the constellation of Fornax. All the objects that are not pinpoints of light in the picture are galaxies of billions of stars. (credit: ESO, J. Emerson, VISTA. Acknowledgment: Cambridge Astronomical Survey Unit)". Finally, at 1:25, the slide changes to "FIGURE 1.15," presenting a "Cosmic Calendar" chart. This calendar compresses the entire history of the universe into one year, showing significant events like the "Big Bang occurs" in January, "Milky Way Galaxy forms" in May, "Dinosaurs become extinct" on December 25, and "Humans appear" on December 31. The detailed caption provides credit information for various parts of the calendar: "Charting Cosmic Time. On a cosmic calendar, where the time since the Big Bang is compressed into 1 year, creatures we would call human do not emerge on the scene until the evening of December 31. (credit: February: modification of work by NASA, JPL-Caltech, W. Reach (SSC/Caltech); March: modification of work by ESA, Hubble and NASA. Acknowledgment: Giles Chapdelaine; April: modification of work by NASA, ESA, CFHT, CXO, M.J. Jee (University of California, Davis), A. Mahdavi (San Francisco State University); May: modification of work by NASA, JPL-Caltech; June: modification of work by NASA/ESA, July: modification of work by NASA, JPL-Caltech, Harvard-Smithsonian; August: modification of work by NASA, JPL-Caltech; September: modification of work by NASA; October: modification of work by NASA; November: modification of work by Dénes Emőke)". The man continues to speak and gesture throughout these transitions.

The video opens with a presentation slide titled "FIGURE 1.15" and an "openstax" logo at the top right. The main content is a calendar depicting cosmic time, where the Big Bang (January 1) to the present day (December 31) is compressed into one year. The upper part of the calendar shows months from January to November, with key events like "Big Bang occurs" (January), "Milky Way Galaxy forms" (May), and "Our solar system forms" (September). The lower part details the month of December, highlighting events like "Vertebrates appear" (December 19), "Land plants appear" (December 20), "Dinosaurs appear" (December 25), "Mammals appear" (December 26), "Dinosaurs become extinct" (December 30), and "Humans appear" (December 31). Throughout the segment, a yellow circular highlight appears and moves to emphasize various points on the cosmic calendar as a man with a beard and short dark hair, wearing a dark short-sleeved shirt, speaks from the bottom right corner of the screen, occasionally gesturing with his right hand. His background shows a room with shelves, books, and other objects. At the 0:37 mark, the slide transitions to a new screen displaying the "openstax" logo and the text: "This OpenStax ancillary resource is © Rice University under a CC-BY 4.0 International license; it may be reproduced or modified but must be attributed to OpenStax, Rice University and any changes must be noted."

The video opens with a man in a blue polo shirt and a headset smiling at the camera, sitting in what appears to be a living room or office with a couch, framed pictures, and other items in the background; a logo for "openstax" is visible in the top left corner and a "logi" logo in the bottom right, before the screen cuts to black at 0:03.
